meta.blurb: Francis of Assisi gave away everything and found joy. Here are the best-loved stories told about him and his friends: a sermon to the birds, a wolf made gentle, and a night of perfect joy in the snow.
meta.bible: The Little Flowers of Saint Francis (in Italian I Fioretti): a collection of stories about Francis and his first friends, written in Italy in the fourteenth century by an unknown author, from older Latin sources; the stories are tradition and legend as well as history. Francis of Assisi: born in Assisi in Italy about 1181, died 3 October 1226 at the Portiuncula, aged about 44; made a saint in 1228. Pietro Bernardone: Francis's father, a rich cloth merchant of Assisi. Assisi: the hill town in Umbria, Italy. San Damiano: the broken chapel near Assisi that Francis repaired; later the home of Clare and her sisters. The Bishop of Assisi: covers the naked Francis with his cloak. Bernard of Quintavalle: a rich man of Assisi, the first to follow Francis. Brother Masseo: tall, handsome and a fine speaker. Brother Leo: Francis's closest friend and helper. Brother Juniper: very simple and kind. Brother Giles: wise, worked with his hands. Brother Ruffino: a gentle friar of Assisi. Brother Angelo: a friar at the hermitage of Monte Casale. The brothers are called the Friars Minor, the little brothers. Pope Innocent the Third: approved the brothers' simple rule about 1209 or 1210. The Portiuncula: the little chapel of Saint Mary of the Angels near Assisi, the brothers' home. Cannara and Bevagna: two villages in Umbria, where Francis preached to the birds. Gubbio: the town in Umbria with the wolf. Brother Wolf: the wolf of Gubbio. Perugia: a town near Assisi. Clare: Clare of Assisi, a noble girl who left home about 1212, founded the Poor Clares, and died in 1253. Saint Anthony of Padua: a gifted preacher and friar, born in Portugal. Rimini: the Italian town by the sea where Anthony preached to the fish. Count Orlando: gave Francis Mount La Verna. Mount La Verna: the mountain in Tuscany where Francis prayed in September 1224 and, his followers believed, received the marks of the wounds of Christ, the stigmata. The Canticle of the Creatures (also called the Canticle of the Sun): Francis's song of praise, about 1225. Brother Sun, Sister Moon, Brother Wind, Sister Water, Brother Fire, Mother Earth, Sister Death. Pope Gregory the Ninth: named Francis a saint in 1228. Where the sources are legend rather than history, the text says 'the story says' or 'tradition says'. Voice and tone: warm, simple and gently humorous, respectful of the Franciscan Christian tradition, never preachy; no gore.

beats.scene: A monk writes by a window with a handful of wild flowers beside him
beats.summary: The Little Flowers is a collection of stories about Francis, gathered in Italy long after his death.

beats.scene: A rich young man in fine clothes laughs among friends in an Assisi street
beats.summary: Francis grows up in Assisi, the rich son of a cloth merchant, who loves parties and dreams of glory.

beats.scene: Francis kneels in a dusty road and embraces a thin, ragged man
beats.summary: Francis changes: he prays in lonely places and, in his own words, learns to love a man he once feared.

beats.scene: Francis carries a heavy stone toward a broken chapel on a green hill
beats.summary: Before the cross at San Damiano, Francis hears a call to rebuild, and he begins to repair the ruined chapel.

beats.scene: Francis stands in front of the bishop in his bare hands, his father furious
beats.summary: Francis gives back his money and his clothes to his angry father before the Bishop of Assisi.

beats.scene: Bernard watches Francis pray through the night beside a bed in a rich house
beats.summary: A rich man, Bernard of Quintavalle, invites Francis to stay and watches him pray all night.

beats.scene: Francis and Bernard open a large book on an altar in a small church
beats.summary: Bernard and Francis open the Gospel three times and each time read about giving up everything.

beats.scene: A group of men in rough brown robes walk together along a country road
beats.summary: More men join Francis, among them Giles, Masseo, Leo and Juniper, and they call themselves the little brothers.

beats.scene: Francis kneels before the Pope in a great hall in Rome
beats.summary: Francis and his brothers go to Rome, where Pope Innocent the Third approves their simple way of life.

beats.scene: A tiny stone chapel stands among huts made of branches and mud
beats.summary: The brothers make their home beside the Portiuncula, a very small chapel near Assisi.

beats.scene: Brother Masseo spins round and round in the road, then falls down dizzy
beats.summary: To choose a road, Francis tells Brother Masseo to spin; Masseo spins until dizzy and falls, facing Siena.

beats.scene: Masseo asks Francis a question while they walk, and Francis answers with a smile
beats.summary: Masseo asks why everyone follows Francis, and Francis says God found no one smaller or weaker than he.

beats.scene: Brother Juniper holds a knife in a wood beside a startled pig
beats.summary: Simple Brother Juniper cuts a foot from a pig to help a sick brother, and its angry owner is later calmed.

beats.scene: Brother Giles hoes a field in the sun, an old book beside him
beats.summary: Brother Giles works with his hands and speaks wise, short sayings.

beats.scene: Francis walks toward a field full of birds near a country village
beats.summary: Walking between two villages, Francis sees a field crowded with birds and goes to speak to them.

beats.scene: Francis speaks to birds in the field, one hand raised
beats.summary: Francis tells the birds to praise God who gave them feathers, air and food, and they listen.

beats.scene: Birds fly off in four directions in the sky, making a cross
beats.summary: At his blessing the birds fly off in four directions, forming a cross, and Francis blames himself for not preaching to them before.

beats.scene: A boy holds a cage of doves while Francis kneels and listens
beats.summary: Francis asks a boy for his captured doves, sets them free and makes them nests; they stay tame with the brothers.

beats.scene: Townspeople of Gubbio hide behind a wall as a huge grey wolf prowls outside
beats.summary: A fierce wolf terrifies the town of Gubbio, and the people go out only with weapons.

beats.scene: Francis walks alone toward the wolf on a rocky path, his hand raised
beats.summary: Francis goes out to meet the wolf, makes the sign of the cross and calls it Brother Wolf.

beats.scene: The wolf lies down at Francis's feet like a gentle dog
beats.summary: The wolf lies at Francis's feet, and Francis tells it that its crimes were wrong but that hunger drove it.

beats.scene: The wolf puts a paw into Francis's hand in the middle of Gubbio's square
beats.summary: Wolf and townspeople make a peace: the people will feed the wolf and the wolf will hurt no one.

beats.scene: The tame wolf walks from door to door in a quiet street
beats.summary: The wolf lives two years in Gubbio, fed at every door; when it dies, the people are sad.

beats.scene: Francis and Brother Leo walk in a cold winter rain on a muddy path
beats.summary: On a freezing winter day, Francis and Brother Leo walk back to the Portiuncula, and Francis speaks of perfect joy.

beats.scene: Francis speaks to Leo, counting on his fingers beside a snowy road
beats.summary: Francis says that even if the brothers healed the sick or raised the dead, this would not be perfect joy.

beats.scene: Francis points to a book and a crowd of listeners on a snowy road
beats.summary: Francis says that knowing all things, or preaching so well that everyone believes, would not be perfect joy either.

beats.scene: Two muddy, shivering friars knock at a convent door while a porter scowls
beats.summary: Francis says perfect joy is to be turned away at the door, in the cold and mud, and still keep patience and love.

beats.scene: A young noblewoman slips out of a grand house at night with a candle
beats.summary: Clare, a noble girl of Assisi, hears Francis preach and leaves home on Palm Sunday night to join him.

beats.scene: Clare and a few women pray together in a small, plain chapel garden
beats.summary: Clare and her sisters make their home at San Damiano, where they live in poverty and prayer.

beats.scene: Villagers run with buckets toward a hillside that seems to blaze with light
beats.summary: Francis and Clare eat together, and villagers who see the woods shining with fire run to help.

beats.scene: Brother Ruffino stands in his undershirt before a laughing crowd in Assisi
beats.summary: Francis sends Brother Ruffino to preach in Assisi in his undershirt, and the crowd laughs.

beats.scene: Francis, also in a plain undershirt, walks into a church beside Ruffino
beats.summary: Francis feels sorry and follows, also undressed, and the townspeople are moved by the two of them.

beats.scene: Two brothers offer a basket of bread and wine to men in a forest
beats.summary: At a mountain hermitage, Francis tells Brother Angelo to take bread and wine to robbers whom he had turned away.

beats.scene: Former robbers in rough brown robes stack wood beside the brothers
beats.summary: Touched by the kindness, the robbers change their lives; the story says they became friars.

beats.scene: Anthony of Padua walks along a river bank beside a crowd at Rimini
beats.summary: At Rimini, people who disagreed with Saint Anthony of Padua refuse to hear him, so he goes to the river.

beats.scene: Many fish lift their heads from the water in rows toward Anthony
beats.summary: Fish of every size gather in rows with their heads above the water, and Anthony praises God for them.

beats.scene: A crowd of townspeople stands on a quay in wonder, hats in their hands
beats.summary: The townspeople run to see and are ashamed; many now listen to Anthony, and the fish swim away after his blessing.

beats.scene: Francis and Brother Leo climb a rocky mountain covered in beech forest
beats.summary: Count Orlando gives Francis Mount La Verna, and Francis climbs it with Brother Leo to pray.

beats.scene: A falcon beats its wings above Francis sleeping on bare ground at night
beats.summary: A falcon wakes Francis before dawn, every day, so that he can pray, and it grows tame.

beats.scene: Francis prays alone on a rock at night under a great field of stars
beats.summary: Francis prays all night, asking two graces: to feel the suffering of Christ and to share his love for others.

beats.scene: A glowing winged figure in the sky above Francis on the mountain at dawn
beats.summary: On 14 September 1224, Francis's followers believed, he saw a winged figure of fire, and marks like wounds appeared on his body.

beats.scene: Francis, weak and tired, rides a small donkey down a mountain path, hands covered
beats.summary: Francis comes down from La Verna ill and half blind, hiding his wounded hands, and Leo cares for him.

beats.scene: Francis sits in a small hut, looking at the sun and moon
beats.summary: Near San Damiano, Francis writes his song of the creatures, calling the sun, moon, wind, water, fire and earth his brothers and sisters.

beats.scene: Francis, lying in his bed, smiles while the brothers listen to him sing
beats.summary: Near the end, Francis adds a verse in praise of Sister Death, and he welcomes it without fear.

beats.scene: Francis lies on bare earth outside the Portiuncula, surrounded by his brothers
beats.summary: Francis returns to the Portiuncula and asks to be laid on the bare earth; he dies on 3 October 1226.

beats.scene: A flock of larks circles over the little chapel roof at dusk
beats.summary: A later story says that at his death a flock of larks circled the roof of the chapel, singing.

beats.scene: Crowds gather in front of a great new church while the Pope speaks
beats.summary: In 1228 Pope Gregory the Ninth names Francis a saint, and a great church is begun in Assisi.

beats.scene: Brown-robed friars walk in pairs along roads in many different countries
beats.summary: The brothers spread across the world, and the Franciscans still live by his example.

beats.scene: Old Clare sits at a window and looks toward the valley of Assisi
beats.summary: Clare lives on for many years at San Damiano and dies in 1253; the Poor Clares still exist.

beats.scene: A book of stories lies open in a garden full of wild flowers
beats.summary: Why the Little Flowers are still read: small stories of kindness to people, animals and all of creation.

A1A2: This book has stories about Francis, a poor man from Assisi.
Francis was born in Assisi, and his father was a rich cloth seller.
Francis changed, and he began to pray and to help poor people.
Francis prayed in a broken chapel, then he started to mend it.
Francis gave back his father's money and even his rich clothes.
A rich man called Bernard let Francis stay in his house.
Bernard and Francis opened the holy book three times to find advice.
More men joined Francis, and they called themselves little brothers.
The brothers went to Rome to ask the Pope for permission.
The brothers made their home near a tiny chapel outside Assisi.
Brother Masseo turned round and round until he fell down.
Masseo asked Francis why all the people followed him.
Brother Juniper loved to help sick brothers, and he did it simply.
Brother Giles worked with his hands and said wise things.
Francis walked to Bevagna and saw many birds in a field.
Francis told the birds to thank God for their wings and food.
The birds flew up in four directions, and they made a cross.
Francis saved some doves and made nests so they could stay safely.
A big, fierce wolf scared everyone in the town of Gubbio.
Francis went out alone to meet the wolf, and he was not afraid.
The wolf lay down at his feet, and Francis spoke to it.
The wolf put its paw into Francis's hand, and it promised peace.
The wolf lived in Gubbio for two years, and no dog barked at it.
One cold winter day, Francis and Leo walked home from Perugia.
Francis said that miracles were not perfect joy, Brother Leo.
Francis said that being wise and clever was not perfect joy either.
Perfect joy, said Francis, is to be treated badly and stay kind.
Clare was a rich girl in Assisi, and she wished to follow Francis.
Clare and her sisters lived at San Damiano, and they prayed every day.
Villagers saw the place shine with fire and ran to help.
Francis sent Brother Ruffino to preach in only his shirt.
Francis was sorry, so he joined Ruffino and preached too.
Francis told Brother Angelo to bring food to the hungry robbers.
The robbers were moved by this kindness, and they changed their lives.
Saint Anthony came to Rimini, but the people did not listen.
Many fish came up and lifted their heads to hear Anthony.
The people were surprised, and many of them listened to Anthony.
Count Orlando gave Francis a mountain, and Francis climbed up to pray.
A bird wakes Francis early each day, so he can pray.
Francis prayed all night, and he asked for two special gifts.
At dawn on 14 September, Francis saw a bright vision in the sky.
Francis came down the mountain, and he was weak and ill.
Francis made a song, and he praised Brother Sun and Sister Moon.
Francis added a new verse for Sister Death, and he was not afraid.
Francis died at the Portiuncula on 3 October 1226.
A later story says that many birds circled over the roof.
Two years later the Pope made Francis a saint in Assisi.
The brothers spread to many lands, and they still exist today.
Clare lived for many more years, and the Poor Clares remain today.
The little stories are still read, and they remind us to be kind.
B1B2: The Little Flowers is a book of stories about Francis of Assisi. It was written in Italy about six hundred and fifty years ago, long after his death.
Francis was born in Assisi about the year 1181, the son of a rich cloth merchant. As a young man he loved parties, fine clothes and dreams of becoming a famous knight.
After a time Francis began to pray in quiet places and to give to the poor. In his own last words he said that he once embraced a sick man he had always feared, and that this changed his heart.
In the ruined chapel of San Damiano, Francis heard a voice from the cross telling him to rebuild God's house. He took the words very simply and began to repair the old walls with his own hands.
Pietro Bernardone was angry that his son was giving his money away. Before the Bishop of Assisi, Francis returned everything, even his clothes, and the bishop covered him with a cloak.
Bernard of Quintavalle was one of the richest men in Assisi. He invited Francis to sleep in his house, and he pretended to sleep while he watched Francis pray through the whole night.
The two men went to a church and opened the Gospel book three times. Each page they found told them to sell what they owned, give to the poor and follow Christ, so Bernard did exactly that.
Soon other men joined Francis, including Giles, Masseo, Leo and Juniper. They wore rough brown robes, lived without money and called themselves the Friars Minor, which means the little brothers.

Francis and his brothers walked to Rome to ask Pope Innocent the Third to approve their way of life. The Pope was unsure at first, but about 1209 or 1210 he gave them permission to live and preach as they wished.
The brothers built small huts of mud and branches beside a tiny chapel called the Portiuncula. It stood in the woods below Assisi, and Francis loved it more than any other place on earth.
At a crossroads Francis told Brother Masseo to spin around like a child and walk where he stopped. Masseo whirled until he was dizzy and fell, and he found that he was facing the road to Siena.
Masseo asked, half joking, why the whole world followed such a plain little man. Francis answered that God had looked everywhere for the smallest and weakest sinner, and had found only him.

The story says that Brother Juniper heard a sick friar long for pig's meat, so he cut a foot from a pig. The angry owner shouted, but Francis spoke kindly, and in the end the man gave the whole pig to the brothers.
Brother Giles worked wherever people needed help, picking olives, carrying water or mending a fence. He spoke few words, but they were wise, and many people came to hear them.
One day Francis was walking from Cannara to Bevagna. Beside the road he saw a large field filled with birds of every kind, and he stopped.
Francis spoke to the birds, reminding them to love and thank God who gave them feathers, a free sky and food without work. They stretched out their necks and opened their beaks as if they listened.

When Francis blessed them, the birds rose into the air and flew away in four directions, like the arms of a cross. Francis went back to his friends, a little sad that he had never preached to birds before.
A boy was carrying some doves he had caught to sell, and Francis asked him to give them away. Francis made nests for them, and the doves laid eggs and lived calmly among the brothers.
A huge, fierce wolf lived near the town of Gubbio. It had killed animals and even people, and everyone was so afraid that they went out only with weapons.
Francis felt sorry for the people and decided to go out and meet the wolf. When the beast ran at him, he made the sign of the cross and called out, “Come here, Brother Wolf.”
The wolf lay down at Francis's feet like a lamb. Francis told it that it had done wrong, but that he knew hunger had made it so cruel.
Francis promised that the people would feed the wolf every day if it hurt no one. The wolf put its paw into his hand to show it agreed, and he led it into the square, where the people also promised.
For two years the wolf went from door to door in Gubbio, and people fed it as if it were a pet. Not even the dogs barked at it, and when it died of old age, the whole town was sad.
One winter day Francis and Brother Leo were walking from Perugia to the Portiuncula. They were cold and tired, and the wind was so sharp that ice hung from their robes.
Francis told Leo that even if the brothers gave sight to the blind or healed the sick, that would not be perfect joy. Leo listened and asked again where perfect joy could be found.
Francis said that even knowing every language or every star would not be perfect joy. Not even preaching so well that the whole world believed would be perfect joy.
Francis said that if the porter drove them away as thieves, and they bore it with love, that would be perfect joy. For him, kindness that survives unkindness was the greatest victory.
Clare was a noble girl of Assisi who heard Francis preach and was deeply moved. Late on Palm Sunday night, about the year 1212, she left her family's house to join him.
Clare and other women made their home at San Damiano, the chapel Francis had repaired. They lived in poverty, prayed all day and welcomed visitors, and Clare led them for forty years.

Francis once shared a meal with Clare at the Portiuncula, and they sat on the ground and talked about God. Villagers saw bright light over the woods and ran with buckets, afraid the church was on fire.
Francis once told Brother Ruffino, who was shy, to go into Assisi and preach to the people, wearing only his underclothes. The crowd laughed at him, and Ruffino felt very embarrassed.
Francis felt sorry for asking so much of his friend, and he followed Ruffino, also in his undershirt. When the people saw both of them, they stopped laughing and began to listen.
Robbers came begging for bread at a hermitage, but Brother Angelo chased them away. Francis told him to take them bread and wine, to find them in the forest, and to ask their pardon.
The robbers ate the bread with surprise and thanks, and the kindness changed their hearts. The story says that they gave up stealing and became brothers themselves.
Saint Anthony of Padua was a famous preacher and a friar. In the town of Rimini, some people would not listen to him, so he walked down to the river and the sea.
The fish swam up in rows, big and small, and lifted their heads above the water. Anthony thanked God for these creatures who had come to listen and had given the people a sign.
The people of Rimini hurried to the water, and they were amazed. Many felt ashamed and came to hear Anthony preach, and the fish swam away after he had blessed them.
A kind noble, Count Orlando, gave Francis a quiet mountain called La Verna. In the summer of 1224 Francis climbed it with Brother Leo and a few others to pray alone.
The story says that a falcon nested nearby and woke Francis every night, a little before dawn, with its cry. Francis thought of it as a friend that helped him pray.
Francis spent the night in prayer and asked God for two gifts. He wanted to feel the pain of Christ as far as a man could, and he wanted to share Christ's love for all people.
His followers believed that at dawn on 14 September 1224, Francis saw a winged figure shining like fire. When the vision ended, the marks of Christ's wounds appeared on his hands, feet and side.
Francis came down from La Verna very weak, and he was almost blind. He hid his hands inside his sleeves, and Brother Leo and the other brothers looked after him with great love.
Ill and nearly blind, Francis made a song of praise in a hut near San Damiano. In it he called the sun his brother, the moon his sister, and the wind, water, fire and earth his family.
Near the end of his life, Francis added a verse in praise of death. He called it a sister, and he said that those who die in peace have nothing to fear.
Francis asked to be carried back to the Portiuncula and laid on the bare ground. There he blessed his brothers, and he died on 3 October 1226 as a psalm was sung.
A story told later says that, as Francis was dying, a flock of larks gathered over the roof of the house. They sang and circled, though larks usually do not fly in the dusk.
In 1228, only two years after his death, Pope Gregory the Ninth declared Francis a saint. A great church was begun in Assisi, and his body was later laid to rest there.
After Francis died, the little brothers spread to many countries, and today they are called Franciscans. They still try to live simply, to care for the poor, and to respect all of nature.
Clare lived for about twenty-seven years after Francis died, and she died in 1253. The women who followed her, called the Poor Clares, are still living in quiet houses around the world.
The Little Flowers are still read because they are short and simple and speak of kindness to all creatures. They do not ask us to be perfect, only to begin with love.
C1C2: The Little Flowers of Saint Francis is a gathering of tales about Francis of Assisi and his friends, set down in Italian late in the fourteenth century by a writer whose name has been lost. Some of its stories are history and some are legend, and the author, like a gardener, simply picked the finest blossoms. We read them today for the light they cast on a man who tried to live without possessions and found joy there.

Francis was born about 1181 in the hill town of Assisi, the son of Pietro Bernardone, a prosperous merchant who dealt in fine cloth. As a young man he was the life of every feast, generous with his money and restless for glory, and he dreamed of winning fame as a knight. Yet something in him was never quite satisfied by the laughter and the noise.

A slow change came over Francis, and he began to seek out lonely chapels, where he stayed for hours in prayer. Near the end of his life he wrote that he had once met a man with a terrible skin disease, a sight he had always dreaded, and had embraced him with compassion. From that moment, he said, what had seemed bitter turned into sweetness of soul and of body.

Praying before an old cross in the crumbling chapel of San Damiano, Francis felt that a voice was asking him to rebuild the house of God that had fallen into ruin. He took the command at its word, begging for stones and carrying them up the hill, and he mended the walls with his own hands. Only later did he understand that a far greater rebuilding was being asked of him.

Pietro Bernardone was furious that his son was spending the family's money on a ruined chapel, and he dragged Francis before the Bishop of Assisi. There, in front of the whole town, Francis handed back his money and even the clothes he wore, declaring that from now on he had only his Father in heaven. The bishop, moved to tears, quickly wrapped the young man in his own cloak.

Bernard of Quintavalle, one of the wealthiest and most respected men in Assisi, was curious about the ragged stranger whom everybody ridiculed, and he invited Francis to spend the night at his house. Pretending to be asleep, he watched his guest rise in the dark and pray for hours, repeating a single phrase of praise. By morning Bernard had begun to wonder whether his own riches had ever made him as happy.

To learn what he should do, Bernard went with Francis to a church, where they opened the Gospel book at random three times. Each page advised the same thing: sell what you own, give it to the poor, and follow Christ without carrying anything for the road. Bernard went home, sold all he had, and distributed the money among the poor of Assisi, becoming the first of Francis's companions.

Others soon followed Bernard's example, among them Giles, Masseo, Leo and Juniper, each quite different from the rest but all willing to live without money or possessions. They wore plain brown robes tied with a rope, begged for their food, and took the name Friars Minor, which means the little brothers. Francis wanted them to remain humble, never grand, and never above anyone they met.

Francis led his small band all the way to Rome to ask Pope Innocent the Third for approval of their way of life. The great churchman was hesitant, for the demands of such poverty seemed severe, but he was won over by the sincerity of the shabby little man in front of him. Around the year 1209 or 1210 he gave his blessing, and the brothers set off with joy.

Near Assisi, in a clearing among the oak trees, stood a small stone chapel known as the Portiuncula, and beside it the brothers built simple huts of mud and branches. Francis loved this humble spot above all places, and it became the true home of his brotherhood, to which the friars returned from their journeys. Whoever came to it, he said, would find that the door was always open.

At a place where three roads met, Francis asked Brother Masseo to turn round and round like a child, and then to walk in whichever direction he faced when he stopped. Masseo whirled until the world swayed around him and he dropped to the dust, and when he looked up, he was facing the road to Siena. Without argument, the two friars set out along it, trusting that the choice was good.

Brother Masseo, who liked to test his friend, once asked why the whole world seemed to run after Francis, though he was neither handsome nor learned nor noble. Francis lifted his face to heaven with delight and replied that God, searching the earth for the smallest and weakest creature, had found nobody more unworthy than he. In this way, he said, God puts the pride of the great to shame.

Brother Juniper was so simple and so kind that he sometimes did foolish things for love, and the story says that he once cut a foot from a living pig to please a sick friar who longed for meat. The owner arrived furious, but Francis scolded Juniper gently and spoke to the man with such patience that his anger vanished. In the end the farmer gave the brothers the whole pig, and everyone laughed.

Brother Giles was a quiet man who believed that honest work was itself a kind of prayer, and he picked olives, carried water and mended fences wherever help was needed. He said little, but his short sayings were so full of good sense that visitors travelled a long way to hear them. Francis loved him, and called him a knight of the Round Table of the little brothers.

Walking one day on the road from Cannara to Bevagna, Francis lifted his eyes and saw a great crowd of birds, of every kind and colour, gathered in a field near the road. He left his companions on the path, hurried into the grass, and began to greet his feathered sisters as though they were an audience. To his great joy, not a single one of them rose from the grass or flew away in alarm.

Francis told the birds, in his gentle voice, that they should praise their Creator, who had given them feathers for clothes, wings for flight, the open air for a home, and food without the need to sow or reap. The birds stretched out their necks, spread their wings, and opened their beaks, as if they wished to show him how closely they were listening. Francis walked among them, touching them with his robe, and not one moved away.

When Francis made the sign of the cross over them, the birds rose together into the air and flew off to the four corners of the sky, so that their paths formed a great cross above the field. Francis returned to his companions full of joy, and also a little ashamed, because he had never thought before to preach to such attentive listeners. From that day, he said, he began to ask all creatures to praise their Maker.

A young man who had caught some wild doves was carrying them to market when Francis, taking pity on the gentle birds, asked him to hand them over. He held them in his robe and promised them that they would not be killed, and then he made nests for them near the brothers' huts. There the doves laid their eggs and fed from the friars' hands, as tame as hens in a yard.

While Francis lived in Gubbio, a huge and ferocious wolf began to roam the countryside, devouring sheep and even, the story says, people who strayed too far from the walls. The townspeople were so afraid that nobody dared to go outside the gates without a spear or a sword, and even then they went in groups. Their daily lives had shrunk to a narrow circle of fear, and the whole valley seemed to hold its breath.

Moved with pity for the townspeople, Francis said that he would go out and speak with the wolf, and, trusting in God, he walked toward its den with only a few anxious friends behind him. When the beast rushed at him with open jaws, Francis made the sign of the cross and called out gently to Brother Wolf, telling him to come near and do no harm. The animal closed its jaws, stopped running, and stood perfectly still, as if it had suddenly remembered how to be gentle.

The wolf lay down quietly at the feet of Francis, as gentle as a lamb, while the saint spoke to it as one speaks to a friend who has done wrong. Brother Wolf had killed and frightened many people, Francis said, and the town was right to be angry, yet he also knew that hunger had driven the creature to such cruelty. Peace, he promised, would be a far better thing for everybody, the hungry wolf as much as the frightened town.

Francis offered a bargain: the townspeople would feed the wolf every day for as long as it lived, if it would promise to harm no one. The wolf bowed its head, lifted its paw, and placed it in his hand, and the two walked together into the town square, where a great crowd had gathered in astonishment. There the people listened carefully to Francis and gave their solemn word that the wolf would never go hungry again.

For two years the wolf lived peacefully in Gubbio, going from door to door, and everyone fed it as if it were a favourite pet, while the dogs, it was said, never even barked. When it finally died of old age, the people mourned it sincerely, because its gentle presence reminded them every day of the miracle of peace. The story ends by suggesting that patient love can tame what weapons and force could never conquer.

On a bitter winter day, Francis and Brother Leo were walking from Perugia to the Portiuncula, their robes so frozen that icicles knocked against their legs. Leo trudged behind, shivering, while Francis strode ahead as though the weather were a pleasant joke. After a while Francis called back to his friend and began to talk about what true happiness really is.

Brother Leo, Francis began, if the little brothers were to work wonders, curing the sick, giving sight to the blind and even raising the dead, that would still not be the perfect joy. Leo, shivering, wrote the words carefully in his heart and asked where such joy could be found, for he could not guess the answer. Francis only smiled in the grey light, pulled his thin cloak around him, and kept on walking through the wind.

Even if the brothers knew every language and every secret of the stars, Francis went on, and even if they preached so beautifully that the whole world was converted, none of that would be perfect joy. Leo was now more puzzled than before, and his teeth chattered in the wind as he asked his friend, almost in despair, to say at last what it was. They had already walked a long way in the dark, and the lights of Assisi were still far off.

Suppose we reach the Portiuncula at last, Francis said, soaked and covered in mud, and the porter calls us thieves and drives us away into the night. If we bear it patiently and without anger, he continued, that would be perfect joy. The grace of Christ, he explained, lies not in what we can do but in suffering for love's sake and staying gentle, and Leo walked on in silence while the cold seemed a little lighter.

Clare, the daughter of a noble family in Assisi, had listened to Francis preach and could not forget his words, and in the night after Palm Sunday, about 1212, she slipped out of her father's house to join him. The brothers met her with torches at the Portiuncula, where Francis cut off her long hair and gave her a plain robe. She was not yet twenty years old, and she had never before spent a night outside her father's walls.

In time other women followed Clare, and together they made their home at San Damiano, the little chapel that Francis had rebuilt with his own hands. They lived in poverty and silence, spent their days in prayer and work, and became known as the Poor Clares, while Clare herself led them with a gentle firmness for about forty years. When her family tried to bring her home, the story says, she simply refused to leave.

Clare once begged to share a meal with Francis, and the brothers set a simple table on the bare ground at the Portiuncula, where the two spoke so warmly about God that the whole company seemed lifted out of itself. The villagers of Assisi, seeing a bright glow over the woods, thought that the church was burning and ran up the hill with buckets. They found nothing burnt, only friars and sisters sitting in quiet joy around the meal.

Francis once told Brother Ruffino, a quiet and shy friar, to go into Assisi without his robe and to preach in the church dressed only in his undershirt. Ruffino obeyed out of love, but the townspeople laughed and joked that the friars were so poor they had lost their wits, and the poor man stood there, burning with embarrassment. Meanwhile Francis, thinking over what he had asked of his friend, began to feel a deep and growing shame.

Francis reproached himself for asking so much of his shy friend, and he hurried to the town, took off his own robe, and stood beside Ruffino in the same humble undershirt. The people saw that the master was ready to share what he asked of his follower, and their laughter slowly faded into respect. He preached to them with such sweetness that many wept, and the town remembered the day for years.

In the mountains of Monte Casale, a band of robbers asked the friars for bread, but Brother Angelo, who thought them wicked, sent them away with hard words. When Francis heard of it, he scolded Angelo for lacking charity, gave him bread and wine, and told him to search the forest for the men and beg their forgiveness. Angelo, humbled and a little afraid, took the food and went off into the forest with a heavy heart.

Angelo found the robbers, laid the bread and wine before them and asked their pardon, and the men, astonished by such gentleness, ate and wept. They said that they had never been treated so kindly, and the story says that they gave up their way of life and joined the little brothers. Francis was heard to say that a loaf given in love is stronger than any sword.

Saint Anthony of Padua, a Portuguese friar and a gifted preacher, once came to the Italian town of Rimini, where a number of people disagreed with his teaching and would not listen to a word he said. Without raising his voice in anger, he walked quietly to the place where the river meets the sea and called to the fishes in the name of God, hoping that somebody, at least, would listen. A crowd of curious townspeople followed him down to the shore to see what on earth he meant to do.

Fish of every size swam up from the deep water and arranged themselves in neat rows, the small ones in front and the great ones behind, all lifting their heads above the waves as if to listen. Anthony praised God for such creatures, who obey their Maker better than some men do, and thanked the fish for coming. They stayed where they were, quite still, until he had finished speaking and given them his blessing.

The word spread through Rimini and the people ran to the shore, where they stared in wonder at the fish gathered like a congregation. Some of those who had refused to listen were ashamed that dumb creatures had shown more attention than they had, and they begged Anthony to preach to them. Only after he had blessed the fish did they swim quietly back into the open sea.

A noble named Count Orlando, who admired Francis, had given him the lonely mountain of La Verna in Tuscany as a place for prayer. In the late summer of 1224 Francis climbed it with Brother Leo and a few other companions. He chose a small hut beneath a beech tree, away from the others, and asked that only Leo should come to him, bringing bread and water once a day.

The story says that a falcon had its nest near Francis's cell, and every night, shortly before dawn, it began to cry and beat its wings until he woke. Francis, who always welcomed small gifts from creation, took it for a friend that watched over his prayers, and he thanked it. When he was ill, the bird, it was said, let the dawn come a little later.

Alone on the mountain, around the feast of the Holy Cross in mid-September, Francis spent a night in prayer, asking two graces before he died. First, he wished to feel, as far as a human being could, the pain that Christ had suffered, and second, to share the immense love that had led Christ to bear it. He prayed on without moving through the cold hours, until the sky above the beech trees began to grow pale.

His followers believed that at dawn on 14 September 1224, Francis saw a being of light with six shining wings descending from the sky. When it vanished, the marks of the wounds of Christ appeared on his hands, his feet and his side. These marks are called the stigmata, and he tried at first to keep them secret from everyone except his closest friends.

Francis came down from La Verna in pain and exhaustion, his eyes weakened by years of illness and tears, and he rode a donkey because he could no longer walk well. He kept his hands hidden inside his sleeves and spoke little of what had happened, and Brother Leo, who had seen more than he ever said, took care of him patiently. He was only about forty-three years old, yet he looked like a man who had already lived two lifetimes.

Ill and nearly blind, lying in a small hut near the chapel of San Damiano, Francis composed in simple Italian a song that has come to be known as the Canticle of the Creatures. In it he praised God for Brother Sun and Sister Moon, for the wind and the clouds, for Sister Water, for Brother Fire and for Mother Earth, who feeds her children with flowers and fruit. He wrote it, tradition says, about the year 1225, in the plain speech of the people rather than in the Latin of the learned.

As his illness grew worse, Francis added a last verse to his song, in which he gave thanks even for Sister Death, from whom no living person can escape. He sang that those who meet her at peace with God have nothing to fear, and the brothers around his bed were astonished at the calm in his voice. It was the courage of a man who had already given everything away and had nothing left to lose or to fear.

Knowing that the end was near, Francis asked the brothers to carry him back to the Portiuncula, and to lay him on the bare earth, so that he might die as poor as he had lived. After he had blessed his friars one by one, he died on the evening of 3 October 1226, while a psalm was being sung beside him. He was about forty-four years old, and he had asked for nothing more than the earth beneath him and the voices of his friends.

A story told by later writers says that, as the evening of his death drew on, a great flock of larks came and circled above the roof of the little house where Francis lay. These birds, which usually avoid the dusk, sang for a long while with unusual sweetness, as if they too wished to say goodbye. Whether or not it truly happened, the tale shows how deeply he was loved by those who knew him.

Only two years after his death, in 1228, Pope Gregory the Ninth declared Francis a saint, in a ceremony in Assisi, before a great crowd of those who had known him. Work soon began on a grand church in the town where he had been born, and his body was later laid to rest within it. Francis, who had owned nothing in his lifetime, was soon remembered in stone and paint all across Europe.

In the years after his death the little brothers travelled far beyond Italy, and their numbers grew until there were friars in most of the countries of Europe and then across the seas. Today they are known as Franciscans, and they still try to live simply, to serve the poor, and to treat the whole of creation with respect. Few religious movements have lasted so long, or spread so widely, from such a small and humble beginning.

Clare outlived her friend by about twenty-seven years, much of it spent in illness, but she never left the quiet house at San Damiano where she had begun. She died in 1253, and her sisters, known as the Poor Clares, have continued her life of prayer in many countries ever since. To the end she remembered Francis as the one who had shown her how to begin.

The Little Flowers have been read for six centuries because they are short and warm and full of gentle surprises, from a sermon to the birds to a wolf who learned to live in peace. They do not demand that we all give away everything, only that we look at the world with tenderness and begin where we are. Francis would have wanted nothing more than for the book to leave its readers kinder than it found them.
